Math 638 - Homework 8.2¶

The Dictator's Dilemma as a Stochastic Feedback Problem¶

This report presents the completed six-part Homework 8.2 experiment.

The stochastic system is

$$ dX_t = a(-X_t+L_t)dt + \sigma dW_t $$

and

$$ dL_t = -\kappa \frac{|X_t|} {1+\eta|L_t|} dt. $$

The controller acts on the perceived deviation

$$ Y_t=X_t-L_t $$

rather than directly on the true state $X_t$.

The baseline parameters are

$$ a=0.5, \qquad \kappa=0.05, \qquad \sigma=0.2, \qquad \eta=1, $$

with

$$ X_0=1, \qquad L_0=0. $$

Executive Summary¶

The completed experiments support five main conclusions.

First, the Euler-Maruyama implementation is internally consistent. The distortion $L_t$ is monotone nonincreasing, and the standardized Brownian innovations have empirical mean essentially zero and variance essentially one.

Second, failure defined by $|X_t|>2$ is common but not universal by the horizon $T_{obs}=100$. The estimated failure probability is about 0.581 and the restricted mean survival time is about 95.31. In the tested local parameter study, reducing $\kappa$ by 25 percent gives the largest increase in restricted mean survival.

Third, the Fokker-Planck equation has diffusion only in the $x$ direction. The distortion $L_t$ is nevertheless random because its finite-variation drift depends on the random process $X_t$.

Fourth, hidden-state reconstruction depends on the observer's information. With exact $Y$, known parameters, and known $L_0$, the synthetic hidden path is recovered to floating-point precision. With unknown $L_0$, the likelihood is broad and the initial distortion is weakly identified.

Fifth, the long-time audit shows that the perceived state can look statistically stable while the hidden pair is not. In the fresh holdout simulation, the perceived process remains order one while $X_t$ and $L_t$ drift together to large negative values.

Validity Audit¶

The final ZIP contains six executed notebooks. Every code cell has an execution count and no notebook contains a recorded execution error.

The numerical outputs agree with the proof-check audit.

The main audit repair concerns Part VI chronology. The revised notebook records an actual LLM response first, fixes its quantitative predictions second, and only then runs a fresh holdout simulation using seed 63862.

No result-changing error was found in Parts I through V.

The final report retains the important limitations:

  • Part II gives a local parameter ranking, not a universal one;
  • Part III gives Monte Carlo support for the weak generator identity;
  • Part IV shows weak identification when $L_0$ is unknown;
  • Part V illustrates observation distortion but does not train a generative model;
  • Part VI provides finite-horizon evidence for an asymptotic heuristic rather than a proof of the asymptotic limit.

Part I - Forward Simulation¶

Euler-Maruyama uses

$$ X_{n+1} = X_n + a(-X_n+L_n)\Delta t + \sigma\sqrt{\Delta t}Z_n $$

and

$$ L_{n+1} = L_n - \kappa \frac{|X_n|} {1+\eta|L_n|} \Delta t, $$

with

$$ Z_n\sim N(0,1). $$

The main experiment uses

$$ \Delta t=0.01, \qquad T=50, $$

and 5000 realizations.

The implementation checks give:

  • maximum observed increment of $L$: -7.265e-12;
  • all final $L$ values nonpositive: True;
  • all observed $L$ increments nonpositive: True;
  • standardized innovation mean: 0.000144;
  • standardized innovation variance: 0.999870.

At $T=50$, the ensemble means are approximately

$$ E[X_T]=-0.5746, $$

$$ E[L_T]=-0.6137, $$

and

$$ E[Y_T]=0.0391. $$

Thus the perceived state can be much closer to zero than the hidden true state.

The sample paths show the distinction between the true deviation, accumulated distortion, and perceived deviation.

Part I Interpretation¶

Because

$$ \frac{|X|} {1+\eta|L|} \ge0, $$

the drift of $L_t$ is nonpositive.

Starting from $L_0=0$, the distortion becomes negative. Therefore

$$ Y_t=X_t-L_t $$

can remain moderate even when $X_t$ has moved substantially in the negative direction.

The controller reacts to $Y_t$, not directly to $X_t$.

Part II - Failure Times¶

Failure is defined by

$$ |X_t|>2. $$

The numerical first-passage time is the first simulation-grid time at which this condition is detected.

Paths that do not fail by

$$ T_{obs}=100 $$

are right-censored.

The main simulation uses 5000 paths and

$$ \Delta t=0.01. $$

The main saved estimates are:

  • failure probability: 0.5808;
  • 95% bootstrap interval: [0.5670, 0.5938];
  • censored fraction: 0.4192;
  • median failure time: 98.09;
  • restricted mean survival time: 95.3132;
  • 95% bootstrap interval for restricted mean survival: [95.1555, 95.4782].

The reported mean is the restricted quantity

$$ E[ \min(\tau,T_{obs}) ]. $$

It is not an unrestricted mean failure time.

The empirical survival curve retains nonfailed paths as censored observations through the common horizon.

Part III - Fokker-Planck Equation¶

For the joint law $p(t,x,\ell)$, the drift components are

$$ b_x(x,\ell) = a(-x+\ell) $$

and

$$ b_\ell(x,\ell) = -\kappa \frac{|x|} {1+\eta|\ell|}. $$

Only the $X$ coordinate contains an independent Brownian increment.

Therefore

$$ \frac{\partial p}{\partial t} = -\frac{\partial}{\partial x} [ a(-x+\ell)p ] - \frac{\partial}{\partial\ell} [ -\kappa \frac{|x|} {1+\eta|\ell|} p ] + \frac{\sigma^2}{2} \frac{\partial^2p}{\partial x^2}. $$

There is no second-order diffusion term in $\ell$.

This does not make $L_t$ deterministic. The path of $L_t$ is random because its finite-variation drift depends on $X_t$.

Because the initial state is deterministic, the initial law is a point mass rather than a smooth density.

A weak formulation uses the generator

$$ A\phi = a(-x+\ell)\phi_x - \kappa \frac{|x|} {1+\eta|\ell|} \phi_\ell + \frac{\sigma^2}{2}\phi_{xx}. $$

The numerical check compares the finite-difference derivative of $E[\phi(X_t,L_t)]$ with $E[A\phi(X_t,L_t)]$.

Test function Finite-difference derivative Mean generator Absolute difference
x -0.193766 -0.200902 0.007135
l -0.016260 -0.016260 0.000000
x^2 -0.132926 -0.132465 0.000461
x*l 0.005444 0.005879 0.000435

The largest discrepancy is approximately 0.0071 for the test function $\phi=x$.

At the chosen Monte Carlo sample size and short derivative interval, that difference is compatible with sampling noise and does not indicate a sign error or missing generator term.

Part IV - Hidden-State Reconstruction¶

The observer sees only

$$ Y_t=X_t-L_t. $$

Since

$$ X_t=Y_t+L_t, $$

the distortion equation becomes

$$ \frac{dL_t}{dt} = -\kappa \frac{|Y_t+L_t|} {1+\eta|L_t|}. $$

This leads to two distinct information regimes.

Regime A - Known initial distortion¶

If the full exact observation history $Y_t$, all parameters, and $L_0$ are known, the equation above is an initial-value problem for $L_t$.

Once $L_t$ is recovered,

$$ X_t=Y_t+L_t. $$

On the matching Euler grid, the saved reconstruction errors are essentially machine precision.

The saved errors are:

  • $X$ RMSE: 1.196e-17;
  • $L$ RMSE: 0.000e+00;
  • maximum absolute $X$ error: 1.110e-16;
  • maximum absolute $L$ error: 0.000e+00.

This is a model-consistency check under exact-model, exact-grid, known-initial-distortion assumptions.

Regime B - Unknown initial distortion¶

Now $L_0$ is unknown over

$$ [-1,1]. $$

The hidden initial $X_0$ is not revealed.

For each candidate $L_0$, the observed increments are evaluated under

$$ dY_t = [ -aY_t + \kappa \frac{|Y_t+L_t|} {1+\eta|L_t|} ]dt + \sigma dW_t. $$

The notebook uses a uniform 801-point grid and normalizes the Gaussian increment likelihood across the grid.

Interpreting these normalized weights as a posterior corresponds to a uniform prior on the candidate grid.

The saved result is:

  • true $L_0$ used only for scoring: 0.0000;
  • maximum-weight estimate: -0.0975;
  • normalized-weight mean: -0.0119;
  • 95% grid interval: [-0.9425, 0.9375];
  • reconstructed $X$ RMSE: 0.1017;
  • baseline $X=Y$ RMSE: 0.1425.

The dynamic reconstruction reduces the displayed $X$ RMSE by about

$$ 28.6\% $$

relative to the naive baseline.

However, the interval is extremely wide, so the initial distortion is weakly identified in this single path.

The first figure shows the broad likelihood over the unknown initial distortion. The second compares the hidden truth, reconstructed hidden state, and naive baseline.

Part IV Interpretation¶

One observed coordinate does not by itself establish nonidentifiability.

With exact dynamics and known initial distortion, the hidden state is determined in this model.

When the initial distortion is unknown, the problem becomes statistical and substantial uncertainty can remain.

Part V - Generative AI Interpretation¶

The analogy is:

true state -> distorted observation -> learned model

Here $X_t$ is the hidden true state while $Y_t=X_t-L_t$ is the observed distorted state.

A learner trained only on $Y$ sees the distribution of $Y$, not the hidden distribution of $X$.

A model can therefore fit the observed data well while still misrepresenting the hidden process.

At $T=20$ using 20000 simulated realizations:

  • mean hidden state $X$: -0.19720;
  • mean observed state $Y$: 0.01816;
  • mean distortion $L$: -0.21536;
  • standard deviation of $X$: 0.20726;
  • standard deviation of $Y$: 0.19378;
  • mean absolute observation distortion: 0.21536;
  • correlation between $X$ and $Y$: 0.97624;
  • Wasserstein distance between the cross-sectional $X$ and $Y$ samples: 0.21536.

The high correlation does not eliminate the systematic difference between the hidden and observed laws.

The distributional comparison shows directly that the data visible to a learner can differ materially from the hidden true-state distribution.

Part V Interpretation¶

Systematic distortion can arise through measurement, reporting, selection, filtering, compression, preferences, or institutional incentives.

A generative model does not automatically recover hidden truth from biased observations.

Part IV also shows that hidden truth is not always unrecoverable. Recoverability depends on the observation mechanism, the known dynamics, initial information, and observation quality.

Part VI - LLM Audit¶

The assignment requires the LLM prediction to be recorded before testing it against simulation.

The original long-time outputs existed before the revised LLM response was inserted, so the corrected audit uses a fresh holdout design.

The final execution order is:

  1. record the independent LLM response;
  2. fix its quantitative predictions;
  3. run a new simulation with holdout seed 63862;
  4. compare prediction and evidence.

The execution counts in the final notebook preserve this order.

Recorded quantitative predictions¶

The LLM predicts, heuristically,

$$ \frac{dU_t}{dt} \approx \frac{\kappa}{\eta} = 0.05, $$

where

$$ U_t=-L_t. $$

It also predicts that the late perceived process behaves approximately like an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process with mean

$$ \frac{\kappa}{a\eta} = 0.1 $$

and variance

$$ \frac{\sigma^2}{2a} = 0.04. $$

The implied standard deviation is 0.2.

It predicts that $X_t$ and $L_t$ drift toward large negative values with approximate slope $-0.05$ while $Y_t$ remains order one.

The response explicitly labels these as heuristics, not proved limits.

Full recorded LLM response¶

The variables have different roles. X_t is the true deviation, L_t is the accumulated distortion, and Y_t = X_t - L_t is the perceived deviation seen by the controller. Since dL_t is nonpositive, L_t decreases from 0 and is generally negative, so Y_t can remain moderate even when X_t and L_t have large negative values.

Brownian noise enters directly only in the X_t equation through sigma dW_t. There is no independent Brownian increment in L_t. Nevertheless, L_t is random because its finite-variation drift depends on the random process X_t.

For a joint density p(t,x,l), the drift vector is b_x = a(-x+l), b_l = -kappa |x|/(1+eta|l|), and the diffusion acts only in x. Therefore the Fokker-Planck equation is partial_t p = -partial_x[a(-x+l)p] - partial_l[-kappa |x|/(1+eta|l|) p] + (sigma^2/2) partial_xx p. At a deterministic initial state this equation should initially be interpreted weakly because the initial law is a point mass.

If the full exact path Y_t is observed, the parameters are known, and L_0 is known, then X_t = Y_t + L_t and L_t solves the path-driven ODE dL_t/dt = -kappa |Y_t + L_t|/(1+eta|L_t|). With the given initial condition this determines L_t uniquely under the usual uniqueness conditions for this ODE, and then X_t is recovered as Y_t + L_t. Thus observing only Y_t does not by itself imply nonidentifiability. If L_0 is unknown, or observations are sparse or noisy, reconstruction becomes a statistical inference problem; uncertainty can remain and should be quantified rather than replaced by a blanket claim of nonidentifiability.

For long-time behavior, define U_t = -L_t, so U_t >= 0 and Y_t = X_t + U_t. Then dU_t/dt = kappa |Y_t-U_t|/(1+eta U_t) and dY_t = [-a Y_t + kappa |Y_t-U_t|/(1+eta U_t)]dt + sigma dW_t. If U_t becomes large while Y_t stays order one, then |Y_t-U_t|/(1+eta U_t) approaches 1/eta. This gives the heuristic limiting equations dU_t/dt approximately kappa/eta and dY_t approximately (-a Y_t + kappa/eta)dt + sigma dW_t. For a=0.5, kappa=0.05, sigma=0.2, eta=1, the quantitative predictions are therefore:

  1. U_t should eventually grow at a rate approaching kappa/eta = 0.05 per unit time, so L_t should drift toward -infinity at approximately slope -0.05.
  2. Since X_t = Y_t-U_t, X_t should also drift toward -infinity at approximately the same slope, while X_t-L_t = Y_t remains order one.
  3. The approximate late-time Y_t process is Ornstein-Uhlenbeck with mean (kappa/eta)/a = 0.1 and variance sigma^2/(2a) = 0.04, so its standard deviation should be about 0.2.

These are asymptotic heuristics, not a proof. In particular, finite-time slopes can be below 0.05 while U_t is not yet large, and numerical agreement over a finite horizon does not establish convergence as t goes to infinity. The main qualitative prediction is therefore a potentially deceptive separation: the perceived state Y_t can look statistically stable while the true pair (X_t,L_t) is not stable and drifts to large negative values.

Part VI Audit Verdict¶

The recorded LLM response passes the required checks:

  1. It distinguishes $X_t$, $L_t$, and $Y_t=X_t-L_t$.
  2. It places the independent Brownian increment only in the $X_t$ equation while recognizing that $L_t$ remains random through its drift.
  3. It gives the correct Fokker-Planck equation.
  4. It distinguishes exact-path reconstruction with known $L_0$ from inference with unknown $L_0$, sparse observations, or sensor noise.
  5. It separates finite-horizon numerical evidence from a proved asymptotic theorem.

The key qualitative conclusion is that a stable-looking perceived state does not imply stability of the hidden pair.

Final Reflection¶

This project illustrates how feedback based on distorted information can make an observed system look healthier than its hidden state.

The first important distinction is between randomness and direct diffusion. Brownian noise enters only the $X_t$ equation, but $L_t$ is still random because it depends on the random history of $X_t$. This is reflected in the Fokker-Planck equation, which contains a second-order derivative only in $x$.

The second distinction is between observability and identifiability. If the exact path $Y_t$ is observed and the parameters and $L_0$ are known, then the distortion equation becomes an ordinary initial-value problem driven by $Y_t$. In that regime, the hidden state is recoverable. When $L_0$ is unknown, the same path gives a broad likelihood over possible initial distortions. Identifiability therefore depends on what information is available, not simply on the number of observed coordinates.

The third distinction is between the true process and the distribution visible to a learner. At time 20, the cross-sectional mean of $X$ is about $-0.197$, while the mean of $Y$ is about $0.018$. The Wasserstein distance between the two simulated distributions is about 0.215. A learner trained only on $Y$ can therefore learn the observed law accurately while remaining systematically different from the hidden law of $X$.

The long-time audit makes this separation stronger. The LLM predicts that $U=-L$ should eventually grow at approximately 0.05 per unit time while $Y$ behaves approximately like an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process with mean 0.1 and variance 0.04. A fresh holdout simulation gives a late-window $U$ slope about 0.04694, mean $Y$ about 0.09306, and variance about 0.03984. At time 500, both $X$ and $L$ have means near $-19$, while the mean perceived deviation remains near 0.093.

The finite-time evidence is therefore consistent with the qualitative picture that the perceived state can appear stable while the hidden pair is not stable.

This is also the main generative-AI lesson. A learned model is constrained by the distribution it observes. If observations are systematically distorted, accurate learning of the observed law does not automatically imply accurate recovery of the hidden truth. Recovering the hidden process requires additional information about the observation mechanism, the dynamics, or the latent state.

Overall Conclusion¶

Homework 8.2 provides a complete stochastic-feedback example in which observation, control, inference, and learning are all affected by information distortion.

The main conclusions are:

  • the forward simulator respects the intended stochastic dynamics;
  • failure-time analysis requires correct treatment of censoring and finite-horizon uncertainty;
  • the Fokker-Planck equation contains diffusion only in the directly Brownian coordinate;
  • exact hidden-state reconstruction is possible under sufficiently strong information assumptions;
  • unknown initial distortion creates substantial statistical uncertainty;
  • the observed distribution can differ materially from the hidden true-state distribution;
  • the LLM's long-time heuristic is strongly supported by the fresh finite-horizon holdout simulation;
  • a stable-looking perceived state can coexist with an unstable hidden pair.

The project demonstrates why a model of observed data and a model of hidden reality are not automatically the same object.
